newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans up sharply on Argentine weather woes.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans up sharply on Argentine weather woes.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures were up half the 30-cent daily limit at midsession amid reports a late-season drought would cut Argentina's soy output and on strong USDA weekly export inspections, traders said.

Floor sources said rumors circulated that a leading U.S. analytical firm had cut its estimates for Argentine soybean production. A weekend cold snap may have nipped late-planted soybeans, further slicing output, traders said.
USDA on Monday put weekly export inspections at 13.8 million bushels, in line with trade expectations for 12 million to 15 million bushels.

While the figure was not surprising, it suggested the export pace was outstripping USDA's expectations. USDA on March 11 pegged 1996-97 U.S. soybean exports at 900 million bushels. Analysts said export inspections needed to drop below 10 million bushels per week to meet USDA's target.

The strong export figure lent support to arguments USDA would have to cut its ending stocks projection from 140 million bushels in Friday's report. Soybeans tumbled on Friday partly on ideas USDA would keep the stocks unchanged.
At 1114 CDT, soybeans were up 15 to three cents per bushel with May up 15 at $8.56.

Gains were limited by speculation a cold, wet spring in the U.S. Midwest would force farmers to switch intended corn acreage to soybeans. Soybeans can be planted as late as July while corn must be in the ground by June.

Funds were active buyers in morning trade after leading Friday's sell-off, floor sources said. Traders said Prudential Securities bought two million bushels May and Cargill Investor Services bought two million May and one million July.
Smith Barney bought two million May, Lehman Brothers bought 1.5 million July and Dean Witter bought 0.5 million July, traders said.
